claims.text: The baseline NbTiAlZrHfTaMoW alloy has a B2 matrix containing antiphase domains and antiphase domain boundaries.
The baseline alloy retains appropriate compressive plastic deformability at room temperature.
The baseline alloy has high compressive-specific yield strength at 1023 K and 1123 K.
Solid-solution strengthening induced mainly by Zr is responsible for the high specific yield strength of the baseline alloy.
The formation and interaction of dislocation slip bands provide substantial plastic-deformation capability in the baseline alloy.
Hf acts as a ductility-promoting alloying element in this NbTiAlZrHfTaMoW system.
Increasing Hf by approximately 1–2 at.% will refine and make the antiphase-domain-boundary distribution more uniform.
Increasing Hf by approximately 1–2 at.% will produce a more homogeneous distribution of dislocation slip bands.
Added Hf will alter local bonding and solid-solution interactions in a way that creates the proposed uniform domain-boundary and slip-band network.
The modified domain-boundary and slip-band network will facilitate dynamic recovery.
Dynamic recovery promoted by the modified microstructure will cause more uniform plastic deformation.
A 1–2 at.% Hf increase will raise ductility and homogeneous strain before failure relative to the untreated baseline.
A 1–2 at.% Hf increase will make plastic deformation more spatially uniform relative to the untreated baseline.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain the baseline alloy's high specific yield strength.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain the baseline alloy's impact-induced energy-release characteristics.
The proposed benefits will occur under quasi-static loading at room temperature and at 1023–1123 K.
The proposed benefits will also occur under dynamic high-strain-rate impact loading.
The beneficial Hf concentration window is limited to approximately 1–2 at.%.
Higher Hf additions may cause coarsening or aggregation.
Microstructural coarsening or aggregation would be detrimental to strength or impact-energy release.
